scores.evidence: Make the cloud database the primary. Start reverse copying to on-prem.
scores.rationale: Mechanisms (CDC, interface-engine queueing, TTL, NIST 800-88, HIPAA 6-year rule) are accurate; minor imprecision like 'audit trails that can't be altered' and lack of depth on reverse-replication limits.

scores.evidence: In practice the switchover may need a short write freeze (seconds to a few minutes).
scores.rationale: Reinterprets zero-downtime sensibly and covers core needs, though generic because it doesn't commit to a specific stack and defers via questions.

scores.evidence: Only one system accepts bookings at any moment.
scores.rationale: Consistent single-writer design with reverse copy; small looseness (reverse copying of a vendor DB, 'hold incoming connection traffic' and users on old read-only).

scores.evidence: run the full switchover at least twice in a pre-production copy, including the rollback. Time each step.
scores.rationale: Targeted tests (rehearsals, shadow, failover, data checks, post-launch daily checks) but with few measurable acceptance thresholds or lag targets.

scores.evidence: It assumes a US hospital (HIPAA), a scheduling app backed by a relational database
scores.rationale: States key assumptions and asks questions, but doesn't say how design changes if wrong; timeline figures are unlabeled beyond 'rough'.

scores.evidence: any data mismatch, connection failure, or failed clinical smoke test means you reverse the DNS and routing changes.
scores.rationale: Covers double-booking, lost messages, forgotten connections, ransomware, but lacks replication lag failure, split-brain/fencing, duplicate message replay, and post-cutover rollback data handling.

scores.evidence: Dashboards: response time, error rates, HL7 queue depth and acknowledgment failures, reminder delivery rates
scores.rationale: Monitoring, command center, hypercare, rollback and IaC covered; incident ownership and ongoing operations are lighter.

scores.evidence: Later improvements: cost tuning, managed services, a FHIR scheduling API, autoscaling.
scores.rationale: Cost is barely addressed beyond a vendor-hosting hint and 30–60 day dual-running; no drivers or estimates.

scores.evidence: Modernize after the move is stable. Don't change the platform and the app at the same time.
scores.rationale: Separates migration from modernization, keeps rollback, and considers vendor-hosted option; identifier/lock-in analysis for managed DB or cloud provider is thin.

scores.evidence: Recommendation for most hospitals: lift and shift, or move to a managed database, with continuous data copying
scores.rationale: Starts with simplest approach and defers modernization; some process elements are generic and the plan is hedged.

scores.evidence: Put the old system in read-only/maintenance mode... Wait until the copy has fully caught up, then run the final data check.
scores.rationale: Phased with weeks and a concrete switchover sequence, but tool choices and criteria are left open and detailed runbook deferred.

checklist.evidence: A Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with the cloud provider is required before any patient data moves.
Test every connection from start to finish in the cloud test environment with realistic (de-identified) messages.
row counts, checksums per table, and business-level checks (appointments per provider per day, open slots, waitlists).
Only one system accepts bookings at any moment.
Rollback trigger: any data mismatch, connection failure, or failed clinical smoke test
a dedicated private link (Direct Connect, ExpressRoute) with a VPN backup. Test latency from clinic workstations
Decide whether you need a second region for disaster recovery.
connect to existing AD and single sign-on. Least-privilege access, multi-factor authentication for admins.
replay peak-hour load, plus a margin, and measure response time from real clinic locations.
Extra support for the first 72 hours, with IT staff on site at large clinics for the Monday-morning peak.
Securely wipe old storage according to NIST 800-88 and keep the certificates of destruction.

traps.evidence: Continuous copying (CDC) from on-prem to cloud
Old and new systems must never both take writes.
A Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with the cloud provider is required before any patient data moves.
Every connection to other systems. This is usually where moves fail
Modernize after the move is stable. Don't change the platform and the app at the same time.

note: Solid, pragmatic single-writer CDC migration plan with rehearsed rollback and interface handling; weak on cost, explicit RPO/RTO, break-glass, and assumption sensitivity, and generic in places.
